name: Alar base reduction (alarplasty)

lead: Alar base reduction removes small wedges of tissue near the nostril wing to make wide or flared nostrils narrower. The payoff is a slimmer-looking nose base, visible once healed.

It is most often combined with rhinoplasty, and on looksmaxxing forums it appears mostly in before-and-after photo threads where posters debate how much change a given face needs. Published research is mainly technique descriptions and classification studies, including work on how the alar region moves during a smile, rather than trials of cosmetic satisfaction.

paras: Small wedges of skin and soft tissue are removed from the nostril sill or the alar-facial junction and the wound is closed, reducing nostril width. It is done on its own or together with a nose job.

As a change to the nostril opening, it has been studied for effects on breathing, and some functional nasal surgery reports link nostril reduction to airflow concerns. Scarring and asymmetry are general surgical concerns. It is performed by surgeons.

angle.text: Alarplasty narrows wide nostrils or a broad nose base by trimming the flare, usually alongside rhinoplasty, and the slimmer base is visible once healed. Forum posters debate how much change a given face needs. Published work is mainly technique reports.

lead: Alar base reduction, usually called alarplasty (or alaplasty), is a cosmetic nasal surgery that narrows the width of the nostril flare or the base of the nose by removing small wedges of tissue at the nostril rim or the alar-facial junction. Wikipedia describes it as removing a wedge of the wing of the nose to change nostril shape, and it can be used cosmetically or functionally.[1] It is performed either on its own or together with rhinoplasty, and surgeons describe it as one of several tools for correcting nostril size and shape.[2][3]

People seek it to make a wide nasal base, flared alae or large nostrils look narrower and more balanced with the tip and the rest of the face; reviews list wide nasal base, alar flaring, large nostril size and nostril or alar asymmetry as the usual indications.[4] In looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who consider their nostrils too wide or flared, mostly in before-and-after photo threads.[5][6]

Published literature on the topic consists mainly of technique descriptions, reviews and classification studies, including work on how the alar region moves during a smile, rather than controlled trials of cosmetic satisfaction.[7][8][4][9]

paras: Surgical papers describe alarplasty as excision of a small amount of skin and soft tissue from the nostril sill, the nostril rim or the junction of the nostril wing with the cheek, followed by suturing, to reduce nostril width or flare. A 2001 article on rhinoplasty in patients whose nostrils appear large relative to a small tip proposed analysing the nostril axis and a nostril-to-tip ratio of about 55:45 (with 60:40 considered acceptable), and described the surgical correction as needing more than one component: lengthening the infralobular segment to increase tip projection, together with nostril sill and alar wedge resections.[2]

A 2026 technique report describes a modified approach in which alar base narrowing and nostril reduction are performed at the same time in Asian rhinoplasty, placing the incision within the natural alar-facial groove and closing with intracutaneous sutures to make scars less visible; the authors reported a significant reduction in the interalar-to-intercanthal distance ratio and mostly imperceptible scars.[10] Surgeons also use alarplasty in functional contexts: one series on external nasal valve collapse used a modified alarplasty combined with columella surgery in severe cases.[11]

Reviews group alar base reduction into three families: cinching sutures that draw the alae together, alar base excisions that remove tissue, and flap advancement.[9] A review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery lists alar wedge excision (an elliptical excision in the alar crease that shortens the alar lobule and reduces frontal flaring), nostril sill excision (which narrows the interalar distance and reduces nostril size) and a combined wedge and sill excision for wide bases with excess flaring.[4] The same authors treat columellar base correction and positioning of the medial crural footplates as a first step, before alar base resection.[4] A separate review notes that nasal base modification is not a routine rhinoplasty step, should be done conservatively to avoid complications such as nasal stenosis, and is best performed last, once the other steps are complete.[9]

A 2018 review by Choi describes modifying the nasal base as a way to refine nostril shape and direction, reduce flaring, narrow the base and balance the two sides, and stresses evaluation of the ala, the supporting lower lateral cartilage and skin condition when choosing a technique.[12] A French article on nostril surgery notes that fear of visible scars makes some surgeons hesitant, and that patients should be told beforehand about the possible scar.[13] A 2014 report describes a Y-V approach to alar base reduction.[14]

A study of a private practice examined how often alarplasty is performed in primary and revision rhinoplasty. In 168 patients operated on between 2004 and 2006 (116 primary, 52 revision), 50 bilateral alarplasties were done, an incidence of 30.2% in primary and 28.8% in revision cases. Non-white patients had a higher overall incidence (63.0%) than white patients (25.4%).[15]

A 2020 systematic review of published nostril surgery cases identified 22 studies covering 1,599 patients: excision techniques were used in 728 patients (45.5%), cinching sutures in 642 (40%), excision with flap advancement in 189 (12%), and a combination of all three in 40 (2.5%). When excessive flaring was present, alar wedge resection was preferred in 92% of cases, and nostril surgery accompanied rhinoplasty in 795 patients.[16]

A 2023 study of 150 Asian women used three-dimensional imaging at rest and during a maximal smile, with three senior plastic surgeons and a clustering algorithm classifying alar movement into three classes. The authors suggest that the least mobile class needs no treatment, the middle class may benefit from optional minimally invasive treatment, and the most mobile class strongly warrants surgery.[7]

Because the procedure alters the nostril opening, surgeons have examined its effect on breathing. A 2026 cross-sectional study in Frontiers in Medicine measured spirometry and respiratory muscle strength in 22 women who had alarplasty at least two years earlier and compared results with predicted normative values. FEV1 percent predicted and the FEV1/FVC ratio were significantly lower than predicted, maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures were reduced, and time since surgery correlated negatively with FEV1 and FVC. The study had no pre-operative baseline.[8] Reports on external nasal valve collapse also note that reducing the nostril opening interacts with airflow, which is why it is discussed alongside functional nasal surgery.[11]

General surgical considerations discussed in the literature are scarring, asymmetry and the risk of overcorrection or nasal stenosis if too much tissue is removed.[9][13] A randomised trial of a modified Doyle splint in 64 patients having alar base surgery with open septorhinoplasty addressed patient discomfort and incision dehiscence at the alar base.[17]

On looksmax.org, alarplasty typically appears alongside rhinoplasty in threads where members post before-and-after photographs and ask others to rate the result.[5] One member asked whether the nostril-narrowing procedure counts as a rhinoplasty and said he wanted it together with a slimmer nasal bridge; another replied that it is not classified as rhinoplasty.[6] These threads treat nostril width as one component of overall nose harmony alongside bridge, tip and projection.[5][6]

Human published work includes a classification study of alar dynamics in 150 Asian women,[7] a technique case series for external valve collapse in 37 patients,[11] a practice-based review of how often the procedure is performed,[15] a systematic review of 22 nostril surgery studies,[16] a technique report with patient-rated scars,[10] a randomised trial of splinting after alar base surgery,[17] and a 2026 cross-sectional study of respiratory function after alarplasty.[8] A 2025 bibliometric analysis catalogued the 50 most-cited alarplasty papers and global research trends.[18] No randomised trial comparing cosmetic outcomes with and without alar base reduction was found.
